scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Cartoon close-up of two gloved hands pressing a burger patty onto a grill, steam rising, the motions deliberately smooth and unhurried — a practiced gesture rather than a cautious one.

scenes.narration: There is a quiet competence in this that you did not expect. In the beginning, every task had edges — you were always slightly afraid of doing it wrong, of forgetting a step, of the headset crackling something you couldn't parse in time. Now the headset is just ambient. You hear the order and your body has already begun before your brain has finished processing. The manager, a woman named Trice who speaks mostly in clipped directives and almost never compliments anyone, told you last week that your ticket times were looking good. She said it while walking past, not stopping, not waiting for a response. You thought about it for the rest of the shift.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Cartoon illustration of a young employee at a grill station glancing sideways over their shoulder, a faint stillness in their expression — not quite a smile, the kind of face someone makes when they've quietly decided something matters.

scenes.narration: Deja has become the person you talk to when nothing in particular is wrong and nothing in particular is right. She works the counter most afternoons while you work the kitchen, and the two of you developed a shorthand early — a look over the partition when a customer is being unreasonable, a specific silence when the fryer alarm goes off for the third time in an hour. On your days off, she texts you things that have nothing to do with the job: a video of a dog that startled itself in a mirror, a complaint about the bus, a question about whether you've seen a show she started. You text back. You are not sure when she became someone you would call a friend rather than a coworker, but the distinction has collapsed, and you don't miss it.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Cartoon illustration of two employees on either side of a service counter partition — one at the register, one at the grill — exchanging a glance over the top, the dining room behind them quiet and empty, the understanding between them wordless and exact.

scenes.narration: What you don't notice yet — what is not yet visible to you as a pattern — is that the job has started to set your clock. You close four nights a week, which means you are home by midnight on the easy nights and by twelve-thirty when something goes sideways, which it does with a regularity that has stopped surprising you. You sleep until ten, sometimes ten-thirty. You eat at two in the afternoon and again at nine at night, before your shift, something quick and filling. The rhythms of everyone you knew before October have become largely theoretical to you. Your cousin called twice in the last month — both times at seven p.m. on a Friday, both times while your hands were in the sink and the headset was still on. You have not called back.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Cartoon illustration of a kitchen clock on a plain wall, its hands pointing to an unusual hour — late night or early afternoon — while outside the small window behind it, the sky is the opposite of what the hour suggests, a muted ambiguity of light and dark.

scenes.narration: There is a version of this that would bother you, and you know it exists, but you haven't found it yet. For now the schedule is just the schedule — a fact as neutral as weather. You are nineteen, now almost twenty, and the structure that the job provides feels less like a cage than like a floor. You know when to wake up. You know where to be. You know what your paycheck will say — four hundred and twelve dollars every two weeks, before the deduction for the health plan you signed up for and have not yet used. There is something in that steadiness that you find, if you are honest, almost comfortable. You are not yet asking what it is steadiness in service of.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Cartoon close-up of a pay stub lying flat on a plain table surface, the numbers legible as amounts without specific text, a hand resting beside it — not picking it up, just near it, as if verifying its presence.

scenes.narration: On a Thursday afternoon in January, midway through a slow shift, Deja shows you how to fold the wax paper so the bottom seam doesn't gap — a small adjustment, a quarter-inch of overlap, the kind of thing that takes three seconds and that you have been doing wrong since October. You redo the last three wrappers in the tray. She doesn't make anything of it. Neither do you. But you will fold wrappers that way from now on, and some months from now you will show someone else, and you will not remember learning it, only that you have always known.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Cartoon close-up of two pairs of hands side by side over a wax paper wrapper — one demonstrating a precise fold at the seam, the other watching and beginning to mirror the motion, both focused downward on the small task.

scenes.narration: By February, you have stopped framing the job as temporary even to yourself. The word sits in your chest somewhere, still technically true, still technically the plan — this is still just until something better comes along — but it has become a kind of furniture rather than a schedule. You don't think about it every day. Some weeks you don't think about it at all. The days move. You get better at things. You clock in, and the smell of the fryer is just the smell of the fryer now — not disorienting, not unpleasant, simply the smell of the place where you spend most of your waking hours. You have stopped noticing it the way you stop noticing the sound of your own refrigerator.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Cartoon illustration of a Burger King kitchen seen from the back, an employee moving through it in relaxed, automatic motion — reaching for a wrapper, turning to the grill, checking a screen — the space fitting around them like a room they've lived in long enough to stop seeing.

scenes.narration: Level three, the architecture.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Flat cartoon illustration of a fast food restaurant floor plan rendered as a blueprint with a small human figure standing at the center, shift schedules and timers orbiting them like planets, in flat bold colors.

scenes.narration: You move apartments in early September, about eleven months in. The new place is a seven-minute walk from the back entrance, which means you stop spending four dollars each way on the bus, which means you stop losing forty minutes each night to sitting in the dark watching the same three stops scroll past. You tell yourself it is a practical decision. It is a practical decision. But practical decisions have a way of settling into the floor of your life and becoming load-bearing, and you do not yet notice that this one has.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Cartoon illustration of a small bare apartment interior at night, moving boxes stacked near the window, the glow of fast food signage visible through the glass casting amber light across the empty floor.

scenes.narration: Your sleep has reorganized itself around the closing shift the way water reorganizes itself around a rock. You are awake until two, sometimes two-thirty, because the adrenaline of the last rush takes an hour to drain. You sleep until ten, sometimes ten-thirty, and the morning is already half-gone by the time you make coffee. This is not insomnia. It is not dysfunction. It is simply the shape that the schedule has pressed you into, and you have pressed back so rarely that the shape has begun to feel like your own.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Cartoon close-up of a phone screen showing a clock reading 10:18, resting on a rumpled pillow, pale daylight coming through curtains that are almost but not fully closed.

scenes.narration: There is a group chat from high school that you have stopped opening. Not because anything happened between you and the people in it — nothing happened, which is almost the point. They are doing things on Friday nights. They send pictures from backyards and apartment parties and a birthday bar crawl someone organized for Marcus, who you have known since eighth grade and whose birthday you remembered only because the phone buzzed the notification at you during a lunch rush. You typed happy birthday and sent it between orders and went back to the line, and that was the extent of it. You are not free on Friday nights. You have not been free on Friday nights in a year.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Cartoon illustration of a young person in a fast food uniform glancing at their phone between tasks at the counter, a group chat notification visible as a glow on their face, the kitchen activity blurred and busy behind them.

scenes.narration: Deja notices before you do. She asks one afternoon in the break room — you are both eating before a close, the cardboard box of fries between you on the metal table — whether you have seen Marcus lately. You say not really. She nods in the way she does when she already knew the answer. You have started to understand Deja's silences as a kind of language: she is not judging you, she is just marking what she sees. This one means: the job is eating the edges of your life, and you are letting it.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Cartoon illustration of two fast food employees in a small fluorescent break room, sitting across from each other at a metal table with a box of fries between them, one looking at the other with a quiet, knowing expression.

scenes.narration: The shift-lead tryout comes up in October, just past your one-year mark. The manager — a tired, not unkind woman named Renata who has been running this location for six years — pulls you aside and says you have the instincts for it. She says it like a compliment, and it is one, and you take it. The raise is a dollar fifty an hour. You do the math in the parking lot on your phone: roughly two hundred and forty dollars a month before taxes, which covers the internet bill and most of the electric, which means you stop going negative the week before payday. You say yes the next morning. You do not think of it as a choice about the future. You think of it as a solution to a specific problem.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Cartoon illustration of a young employee standing in a fast food parking lot at dusk, looking down at their phone with a calculating, quietly resigned expression, the restaurant windows glowing behind them.

scenes.narration: The weeks between saying yes and the actual tryout have a particular texture to them — you are watching yourself more closely, which means watching everyone else more closely, which means you start to notice the things Renata notices. The new hire who holds the wrapper wrong. The order that sits twenty seconds too long under the heat lamp. You already knew these things the way your hands know them, but now you are translating them into something you could say out loud to someone else. It is a different kind of knowing, and you are surprised to find you are good at it.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Cartoon close-up of gloved hands demonstrating the correct fold on a burger wrapper to a second pair of hands, the paper crisp and precise, a ticket printer curling a new order just at the edge of the frame — a deliberate echo of the same hands from an earlier level, now in the instructing position.

scenes.narration: By November you have the shift-lead badge clipped to your collar and a new section of the schedule to sign off on, and the job has quietly become something larger than it was. Not larger in the way of ambition — larger the way a piece of furniture becomes larger when you have moved it to the center of a room. Everything else has arranged itself around it. Your sleep. Your apartment. Your Fridays. The version of yourself that was going to be here only temporarily has been gone for a while now, and you have been too busy to hold a funeral for it.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Cartoon illustration of a fast food restaurant floor plan seen from above, the central cooking station glowing warmly, furniture and objects in a small apartment arranged in the surrounding space as if orbiting it — bed, coffee maker, calendar — all angled subtly toward the restaurant at the center.

scenes.narration: There is a night in late November — a slow Tuesday, the kind where the drive-through goes quiet for twenty minutes at a stretch — when you stand at the back door and look out at the parking lot. The orange lights are on. There is one car parked crookedly near the dumpster. The air smells like cold concrete and fryer grease and, faintly, the dumpster. You are twenty years old. You have been here a year and one month. You go back inside before the thought fully forms, because there is a grill to scrub and a close to finish, and that is enough.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Cartoon illustration of a young fast food employee standing at an open back door, looking out at an empty orange-lit parking lot at night, their posture still and unresolved, the warm kitchen light spilling out around them into the cold.

scenes.narration: Level four, the long middle.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of the interior of a Burger King kitchen at mid-afternoon, warm amber light from the fryer, a single employee standing at the grill with their back to the viewer, the dining room visible through the pass-through window, empty and still.

scenes.narration: It is the second year now, and you have stopped thinking of the job as something happening to you. The lunch rush comes in like weather — you can feel it before the first car pulls into the drive-through, something in the air pressure of the place, the way the headset goes quiet for exactly thirty seconds and then doesn't. You shift gears the way you shift gears driving — without naming the gear. The new hire at the fry station is doing the thing where they try to manage two baskets at once before they're ready, and you don't say anything yet, just watch, and you already know what the oil burn on their forearm is going to look like tomorrow.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Cartoon illustration of a Burger King drive-through window from inside, a line of cars visible through the glass, an employee in a headset leaning slightly forward in anticipation, the kitchen behind them already in motion — tickets curling from the printer, fryer baskets rising.

scenes.narration: You are twenty-one in the spring of the second year, and you are training a kid named Marcus who is seventeen and convinced he will be out in two months. You show him how to fold the wrappers without tearing them — the same motion Deja showed you, thumbs first, a slight roll at the top — and he nods with the polite impatience of someone who thinks the lesson is unnecessary. You let him think that. You have learned that the lesson lands later, or it doesn't, and either way the line keeps moving.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Cartoon close-up of two pairs of hands at a prep counter — one in a worn uniform with practiced stillness, one in a newer uniform slightly tensed — both working a burger wrapper, the older hands demonstrating a clean fold, wax paper catching the overhead light.

scenes.narration: There are rituals now, and you have stopped noticing that you depend on them. The free meal before a close — you always take the same thing, a Whopper with extra pickles and a large water, eaten standing at the edge of the prep counter in the twenty minutes between the dinner rush and the long drag toward midnight. The particular satisfaction of scraping the grill clean at end-of-night, the sound of the scraper against the flat iron, the smell of old grease lifting off the surface in a pale curl of smoke. These are not the things you would have named, at nineteen, as reasons to stay. But they are the things that make staying feel less like waiting.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Cartoon close-up of a metal grill scraper drawn back across a flat-top grill, a clean stripe of silver appearing behind it in the dark surface, the surrounding kitchen dim and quiet, a single overhead light casting the motion in warm shadow.

scenes.narration: The 3 a.m. closings with Deja are something else entirely. Someone puts on music from their phone — it changes week to week, whatever she is into, something with a beat you can mop to — and the dining room turns into a different place. Chairs flipped up on tables, the yellow mop water catching the fluorescent blue-white, the two of you working around each other without talking much because you have been talking all night and now it is just the work and the music and the particular exhaustion that has looped back around into something like peace. By two-thirty you are both done and you stand at the back door for a minute before you go out, neither of you ready to leave yet, neither of you saying so.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Cartoon illustration of a fast food dining room at 3 a.m. — chairs flipped onto tables, two employees mopping in the blue-white fluorescent light, one glancing over their shoulder mid-laugh, the room quiet and geometric around them, a phone glowing faintly on the counter in the background.

scenes.narration: Somewhere in the second year you had a tab open on your phone — a community college page, a logistics certificate, something you'd read about that seemed manageable — and one night after a close you closed the tab without meaning to, and you never went back to find it. This is not a story you tell yourself as a failure. You were tired. You were making nine-forty an hour and the rent on the studio had gone up sixty dollars in January and the math was the math. You keep meaning to look again. You keep meaning to look again.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Cartoon illustration of a young fast food employee sitting on the edge of a plastic chair in the break room after a close, still in uniform, looking down at a phone screen with a tired, half-present expression — the room behind them bare and fluorescent-lit, a coat on a hook, a half-drunk water bottle on the table.

scenes.narration: The second year folds into the third the way the months fold into each other when the schedule never really changes — not abruptly, not with ceremony, just a Tuesday that looks like the Tuesday before it and the Tuesday before that. Marcus has gotten good at the grill. He no longer tears the wrappers. He has also stopped talking about the two months, which you notice without comment. The lunch rushes are no longer a test of anything. They are just Tuesdays.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Cartoon illustration of a long wall of identical shift schedule pages pinned to a corkboard, each page slightly yellowed at the edges, a single small figure standing before the board with one hand raised toward it — the schedules stretching in both directions past the frame, a quiet sense of accumulation without beginning or end.

scenes.narration: You are twenty-one going on twenty-two and you are good at this job in a way that is no longer surprising or particularly interesting to you. You know where every tool is without looking. You know which regulars want their coffee already doctored and which ones will tell you again anyway. You know how to read the manager's mood from forty feet away and adjust accordingly. This is not nothing. You know that it is not nothing. But it is also not what you thought you were building toward, back when you thought you were building toward something specific, back when the job had an end date that kept getting erased and rescheduled and finally, quietly, never rescheduled again.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Cartoon illustration of a fast food employee behind the front counter, facing the dining room — posture easy and settled, one hand resting on the counter, expression calm and unreadable — the room around them familiar and unremarkable, morning light coming in low through the front windows, a coffee cup waiting on the pickup ledge.

scenes.narration: Level five, the cost.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] A cartoon illustration of a lone Burger King employee standing at the back door of a fast food restaurant holding two trash bags, the empty parking lot orange-lit behind them, looking out at nothing in particular with a still, unreadable expression.

scenes.narration: It is a Wednesday in February, somewhere in your third year, and Deja tells you before the lunch rush so you will have something to do with your hands while she says it. She has been accepted into a radiography program in Dayton. She starts in the fall. You tell her that is incredible, and you mean it — you can hear yourself meaning it — but there is a half-second between the words and the meaning where your mind does a calculation you don't want to name. You have known Deja for two and a half years. You did not know she was applying anywhere.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] A cartoon close-up of two employees in uniform standing side by side at a prep counter, one turned slightly toward the other mid-conversation, the other's hands still on the counter, neither fully facing the viewer, the fryer glowing amber at the edge of the frame.

scenes.narration: The going-away cake comes from the grocery store two doors down — white frosting, the kind that tastes faintly of shortening. Someone has written her name on it in blue gel. You eat a slice in the break room on your fifteen, standing up, and Deja is laughing at something the new manager said, and she looks the way people look when a door is already open behind them and they have one foot through. You take a photo of her with the cake. You are twenty-two years old, standing in a break room that smells like fryer oil and old coffee, and you smile in the photo too.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] A cartoon illustration of a small break room with a sheet cake on a folding table, a few employees gathered around it in uniform, one person laughing with their head tilted back, fluorescent light overhead, the scene warm and ordinary and a little cramped.

scenes.narration: Her last shift is a Sunday close. You do the 3 a.m. cleanup together one final time, and nobody puts music on, and you mop your section and she mops hers and the dining room chairs are all flipped up on the tables the way they always are, and the blue-white fluorescent hum is exactly what it has always been. There is not much to say that hasn't already been said. You hug her in the parking lot at quarter past three and watch her get into the car, and then the car is gone, and then the parking lot is just a parking lot again.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] A cartoon illustration of a fast food kitchen at 3 a.m., one employee mopping alone in the blue-white fluorescent light, the dining room chairs silhouetted on tables behind them, the space that was recently occupied beside them now noticeably empty.

scenes.narration: The new hire comes in two weeks later. Her name is Brianna, and she is seventeen, and on her first shift she tears three wrappers trying to fold them. You show her the technique — thumbs anchored, fold from the bottom, press at the seam — and while you are showing her you hear yourself using the same words Deja used on you, in more or less the same order. You notice this the way you would notice a small sound from a room you thought was empty. Brianna gets it by the fourth try. She says thank you. You tell her it takes a few days.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] A cartoon close-up of two gloved hands demonstrating a burger wrapper fold over a prep counter, a second pair of younger hands watching closely nearby, a torn wrapper pushed to the side, the motion mid-gesture and focused.

scenes.narration: You have a savings account with four hundred and thirty-seven dollars in it. You know this number because you checked it on your phone during your break last Thursday, sitting on the curb behind the restaurant with a cup of fountain water, the cold concrete coming through your work pants. You have been meaning to move that number for a long time — to make it the beginning of something rather than just the total. But the check-engine light came on in March. The security deposit on the apartment went up in January. The next thing has a way of arriving before the last one finished.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] A cartoon illustration of an employee sitting on a curb behind a restaurant in work uniform, a paper cup of water beside them, phone face-up in hand, the back wall of the building looming behind them, the afternoon light flat and pale.

scenes.narration: The months between Deja leaving and where you are now have a different texture than the ones before. The rituals are the same — the free meal before a close, the clean grill, the particular satisfaction of a lobby that has been reset to zero — but they belong to you alone now in a way they didn't before. There is no one beside you who knows what they cost. Brianna is a fast learner and a decent person, and you like her well enough, but it is not the same thing, and you understand now that it was never going to be.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] A cartoon illustration of a fast food counter at the end of a shift, everything wiped clean and returned to order, a single employee standing back to observe the emptied space, the dining room dark beyond the counter glass, the kitchen amber-lit behind them — the stillness of a room set for something that has already happened.

scenes.narration: You are twenty-two. When you first clocked in — three years ago, a Thursday in late October, the fryer smell arriving before you were through the door — you were certain you would not be here at twenty-two. Not as a judgment of the place, just as a fact about time: there would be other things between then and now, and this would be one of the early ones. But time moved the way it moves, and the schedule held, and you are still here. This is not a tragedy. It is, at the moment, simply true.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] A cartoon illustration of a young employee in uniform standing just inside the back door of the restaurant, hand still on the door handle, the orange-lit parking lot visible through the gap behind them, their expression still and inward — not devastated, not resigned, just present in a way that carries weight.

scenes.narration: Level six, the reckoning.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of a Burger King employee uniform hung neatly on a hook against a plain wall, the paper crown balanced on top, a single warm amber light casting a long shadow across the floor — still and quietly monumental.

scenes.narration: It is a Tuesday in November, and you are twenty-three, and nothing unusual is happening. The lunch rush came and went. The grill is clean. Someone refilled the napkin dispensers without being asked. You are standing at the back counter with a cup of water and there is no crisis in front of you, no ticket backed up, no manager hovering — just the ordinary hum of the place in the late afternoon, the fryer cycling, the walk-in door exhaling cold air, the dining room holding its usual two or three people who are not really here for the food. You are not having a revelation. You are just noticing, for the first time in a while, that you are here.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of a fast food kitchen in the mid-afternoon lull, a lone employee leaning against the back counter holding a paper cup of water, the grill gleaming, the fryer pilot light steady, the dining room faintly visible through the pass-through window — ordinary and quiet.

scenes.narration: You think about Deja. It has been four months since the going-away cake, since the grocery-store frosting that was too sweet, since you watched her load her car in the back lot with two duffel bags and a box of textbooks. She texts sometimes — not often, but enough. A photo of her campus in the snow. A complaint about an exam. Nothing about wrappers or timers or headsets. You texted back each time, something short and warm, and then you went back to the line. You are glad for her. That is the whole and uncomplicated truth of it.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of a phone screen showing a text thread — no readable text visible, only the warm glow of the screen held in a gloved hand, a blurred kitchen behind it, the suggestion of a late-night shift still in progress.

scenes.narration: You try, in the quiet of the Tuesday afternoon, to count what the job has given you. And the list is longer than you expected when you first walked in at nineteen thinking the smell would be temporary. You know how to manage seven things at once without panicking. You know how to de-escalate a man who is angry about pickles and is actually angry about something else entirely. You know how to read a room from the sound of it — the particular pitch of a backed-up line, the specific silence before someone quits mid-shift. These are not small things. They are not the things you planned to learn, but you have them now, and they are yours.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of a fast food employee at the counter, seen from a slight distance, hands resting still for once, facing the dining room with a calm and unreadable expression — a figure who has learned to hold a space without effort.

scenes.narration: And then the other count. The nights you said no to things because you closed Sunday and opened Monday and there was no space in between. The resume that lived for two years in a folder you stopped opening. The semester you were going to enroll in — you had the catalog, you had a highlighter, you had a Tuesday evening free — and then the schedule shifted, and the enrollment window closed, and you told yourself next term. Next term was six terms ago now, and at some point you stopped using the word next. You didn't decide to stop. The word just lost its grip.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of a small desk in a dim apartment bedroom, a closed folder sitting on it with a highlighter resting across the top, a calendar on the wall with months partially visible — dust on the surface, warm lamp light from the side, the feeling of a room that has been waiting.

scenes.narration: What you cannot quite work out — standing here in the lull, the fryer cycling, the afternoon going orange outside the drive-through window — is whether the version of you that walked in at nineteen made a choice or simply moved through the only door that was open. You remember thinking just until something better comes along. You remember the phrase as clearly as you remember your first headset, the foam worn thin on one ear. What you cannot remember is the moment you stopped believing the something-better was still coming, because there was no moment. It was not an event. It was a gradual adjustment, like your eyes adjusting to a room you've been in for years.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of a drive-through window from the inside, the orange late-afternoon light pressing through the glass, the employee's reflection faint in the pane — a face half-present, half-absorbed into the warm light outside.

scenes.narration: The new hire — Marcus, twenty and from the north end of the city, who folds the wrappers wrong the same way you once did, who is definitely not staying past spring — has started to relax into the shift. You noticed it last week. The first three weeks he moved like someone who expected to be corrected, who held his body apologetically. And then one day he didn't. He started moving through the kitchen like it was a place he understood, and you recognized the moment because it was once yours. You didn't say anything. You just handed him the next order.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of two employees working the grill side by side — an older one moving with ease and economy, a younger one beginning to match the rhythm, both focused on the line in front of them, the kitchen lit warm and functional.

scenes.narration: The shift ends. You do the close — the grill, the counters, the mop, the bags — and you do it the way you have done it a thousand times, efficiently and without thinking about it, which is its own kind of grace. You pull the two trash bags from the bins by the back door, one in each hand, the plastic handles cutting slightly into your palms the same way they always do, and you push the door open with your shoulder and step out into the parking lot.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of a fast food employee pushing open the back door of a restaurant with their shoulder, both hands holding heavy trash bags, the door swinging into the night air — the interior warm and fluorescent behind them, the outside dark and beginning.

scenes.narration: The parking lot is empty and orange-lit — the same sodium glow it has always been, the same asphalt, the same dumpster enclosure with one hinge that doesn't quite close. You stand there for a moment with a bag in each hand, not moving yet. The night is cold in the particular way that November nights are cold, without drama, just settled. You are twenty-three years old and you have been standing in this exact spot, in this exact posture, more times than you could name. And for a moment you are not sure how many years it has been since the first time you stood exactly here — nineteen and certain you were passing through, the smell of the fryer in your hair, your feet already sore, the night in front of you like an open question you hadn't learned to read yet.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of a lone fast food employee standing at the back door of the restaurant in a cold November night, a trash bag in each hand, the empty parking lot stretching out in front of them under orange sodium light — small against the open lot, still, looking at nothing in particular.

scripts.title: Your Life As A Full-Time Burger King Employee
scripts.topic_description: You start by clocking in, learning the rhythm of grills and timers, and taking orders with a practiced smile. The middle drifts through impossible lunch rushes, quiet 2 a.m. cleanups, and the small economies of tips, breaks, and friendships; the architecture of the job is a choreography of signage, ticket printers, and grease. The arc closes on a quiet reckoning — what this steady grind has bought you and what it has quietly taken away.

scripts.script_title: Your Life As A Guard On Death Row

scenes.narration: Level one, the manual.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of a lone guard in a dark olive uniform standing in a long institutional corridor, fluorescent overhead strips casting hard flat light on pale green walls, heavy steel cell doors receding into the distance on both sides, the guard's silhouette small and centered against the deep vanishing point.

scenes.narration: You are twenty-four years old, and the uniform smells like dry-cleaning fluid and something else — a pressed institutional optimism, the smell of a thing that has never been worn in earnest. The manual says to maintain a minimum of three feet between yourself and the bars at all times. It says this in the same neutral font as everything else. You read it twice on the bus ride in, the morning of your first shift, in November, and you think: that seems reasonable.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Flat cartoon close-up of a dark olive uniform jacket laid flat, collar neat, a small laminated identification badge clipped at the chest, the fabric slightly stiff, a single overhead fluorescent tube reflected in the badge surface.

scenes.narration: The senior officer who walks you through orientation is named Briggs. He is forty-one and has the flat cadence of a man who has explained the same things so many times they have stopped meaning anything to him and started meaning something else — a kind of private shorthand for the shape of his entire adult life. He shows you the count procedure first. How you move your eyes across each cell, how you wait for the acknowledgment, how you mark the clipboard. He says: the count is not bureaucracy. The count is the floor you are standing on. You nod. You do not yet know what he means.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of two figures in dark olive uniforms standing in a corridor — a younger Black man with close-cropped hair and broad shoulders, and an older figure beside him, both facing a row of closed steel cell doors, the older figure gesturing toward the doors with a clipboard.

scenes.narration: The unit has its own vocabulary, and you begin absorbing it the way you absorb any new language — first the nouns, then the verbs, then the grammar that governs the space between them. There is the tier, which is the corridor. There is the count, which happens at 4 a.m. and again at noon and again at 6 p.m. There is movement, which means authorized transit from one part of the facility to another. There is the phrase secured and the phrase cleared and the phrase that one's quiet tonight, which Briggs says the first Wednesday you work together, and which you will hear said again and again across years until it becomes indistinguishable from a prayer.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of a long institutional corridor at night, fluorescent overhead strips humming pale white light onto pale green walls, a lone guard figure — Black man, close-cropped hair, dark olive uniform — walking the tier with a clipboard, the cell doors evenly spaced on either side, receding into flat shadow.

scenes.narration: The physical geography of the unit takes about two weeks to stop feeling unfamiliar. The key ring weighs eleven ounces — you weigh it once on a postal scale in the break room, just to have a number to hold — and within a month you no longer feel it on your hip. You learn where the fluorescent tube on the far end of the tier flickers twice before it stabilizes, always exactly twice, and you begin to find this reliable in a way that pleases you without your being able to say why. The distances become automatic. Three feet from the bars. Then five. Then you are standing at the exact right distance without thinking about standing at all.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Flat cartoon close-up of a heavy institutional key ring resting on a break room table surface, a dozen keys of varying sizes fanned out against the institutional laminate, a paper coffee cup beside it, overhead fluorescent light flat and even.

scenes.narration: The men on the unit are referred to in the manual as residents, which is a word you notice precisely once and then stop hearing. They are mostly quiet in the mornings. Some of them have photographs taped to the walls of their cells — small squares of ordinary life, children and grandmothers and dogs, things that look slightly wrong in the flat overhead light the way all photographs look slightly wrong when the place they were taken no longer exists. One man asks you, during your third week, if you can check whether his appeal paperwork went out. You tell him you will look into it. You do look into it. This will not always be the kind of thing you can do anything about, but you do not know that yet.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of a guard — Black man, close-cropped hair, dark olive uniform, square jaw, steady dark eyes — standing just outside an open cell door, weight slightly forward, listening, a man's hand visible through the bars gesturing in the middle distance, the guard's expression neutral and present.

scenes.narration: By December — six weeks in — you have run the count enough times that your body knows the route before your mind instructs it. You walk the tier at 4 a.m. and there is a specific quality to that hour, a compression of sound, like the building is holding something in. The cells are mostly dark. You count the shapes in them. Shape, acknowledgment, mark. Shape, acknowledgment, mark. It is a procedure and procedures are knowable and the knowable is a form of safety, and you are twenty-four years old and you mistake the procedure for the thing the procedure is meant to contain.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CONTINUOUS] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of a guard walking a night tier, overhead fluorescent light casting flat pale pools at intervals, the figure moving through light and shadow in sequence, clipboard in hand, each cell door a dark vertical rectangle.

scenes.narration: There is one man on the tier who laughs at something through his cell door one afternoon — a short, genuine sound, the kind of laugh that happens before the person remembers where they are. You do not know his name yet. You will. For now he is a voice and a number and a shape in a dark cell at 4 a.m., and the unit is orderly, and the manual is a thing you have read and understood, and the job feels like something you can be good at. You are still learning the difference between a floor and a foundation.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of an empty institutional corridor in flat midday fluorescent light, pale green walls, a row of closed steel cell doors, the corridor itself perfectly symmetrical — the floor a flat gray plane stretching toward a vanishing point, the overhead light even and sourceless, nothing out of place.

scenes.narration: Level two, the rhythm.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of a guard walking a long cell-lined corridor at night, dim blue overhead light, the guard's silhouette moving past evenly spaced barred doors, a faint warm glow from one cell suggesting a lamp or a small television.

scenes.narration: Somewhere in the third month, the manual stops being something you consult and starts being something your body already knows. You do the 4 a.m. count before you are fully awake — key ring in the left hand, clipboard angled against the corridor light, your pace exactly measured without your measuring it. The fluorescent strip above cell eleven flickers at the same half-second interval it has flickered since your first week, and you no longer notice it until the night it doesn't.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon close-up of a guard's left hand holding a heavy ring of keys, the keys slightly motion-blurred, a clipboard visible at the edge of the frame, pale institutional light from above.

scenes.narration: By the fifth month you know the tier by its sounds before you turn the corner. There is a man in cell four who always clears his throat at 3:50, precisely, as if preparing to say something he will not say. There is a man in cell nine who sleeps with the television on at a volume just below audible, so that you catch the rhythm of it — the percussion of the laugh track, the swelling of the score — without ever hearing the words. You begin to understand that the tier runs on a schedule that has nothing to do with the one in your manual, and that your job is to hold both at once.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Flat cartoon illustration of a long institutional corridor at 4 a.m., cell doors receding into shadow, a faint television glow pressing blue-white through the bars of one cell near the far end, the corridor otherwise still.

scenes.narration: The key ring weighs fourteen ounces. You know this because you weighed it once, on the postal scale in the mail room, the afternoon a supervisor asked you to cover a second shift and you needed something to do with your hands. Fourteen ounces. Less than a pound. You carry it for eight hours and by the end of the shift your hip has a dull ache that you do not tell anyone about, because nobody tells anyone about it — it is just part of what the job weighs, and not the heaviest part.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Flat cartoon close-up of a heavy key ring resting on a small institutional scale, the scale's needle slightly past center, the keys splayed in an uneven ring, the surrounding surface worn pale linoleum.

scenes.narration: The routines accumulate the way months do — without ceremony, without announcement. You run the count. You log the check. You walk the tier. You run the count again. You do this across a winter and into a spring and the rhythm of it has the quality of something that was always true, as if you cannot remember learning it, only knowing it. The manual said to maintain three feet from the bars. You no longer think about the three feet. You simply keep them.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CONTINUOUS] Flat cartoon illustration of the same corridor section across a span of time — the light shifting from cold night-shift blue to the gray of early morning, then to the flat white of a full day shift, then back to blue, the cell doors unchanged, the fluorescent strip above cell eleven flickering slightly in each frame.

scenes.narration: It is a Tuesday in late April — you are almost seven months in — and a man in cell seven calls out as you pass. Not loudly. The way someone calls out when they have been waiting, not urgently, just steadily. He says he needs an extra blanket because the vent above his cell runs cold all night. You log it. The blanket arrives two days later, because that is how the blanket arrives — two days later, through channels, correctly. He thanks you and you nod, and neither of you makes anything of it. But you begin to notice that you know his voice before his face now. That has happened without your deciding it would.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell — Black man in dark olive correctional officer uniform, close-cropped hair, steady expression — pausing mid-stride in the corridor, turning slightly toward a cell door, clipboard held loosely at his side, his posture unhurried.

scenes.narration: There are eleven men on the tier. You learn them the way you learn a building's layout — practically, usefully, without sentiment. Cell two sleeps until seven and then reads. Cell five paces from eight to ten, always, without variation. Cell nine with the television. Cell eleven with the flickering light above his door, which is not his fault and not yours and simply is. You know who asks for things and who never does, and you have begun to understand that the men who have stopped asking are often the ones worth watching closest. This is not in the manual. It is in the tier.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Flat cartoon illustration of a corridor viewed from one end, eleven cell doors visible in perspective, each slightly different — one with a dim lamp glow, one dark, one with the faint blue of a television, the overhead strips casting flat even light between them.

scenes.narration: The man in cell three — Curtis — has been on the tier for four years before you arrive. He is forty-one and reads paperback novels that come to him through the chaplain, two at a time. By your eighth month he is calling you by your first name. Darnell. Not to provoke anything. Just the way a person uses a name when they have decided the person attached to it is worth the effort of knowing. You do not correct him. You tell yourself it is because it costs nothing, because the corrections you save for things that matter. But the truth is simpler: it is the first time since your first week that anything on the tier has felt like a choice made freely.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon close-up of a worn paperback novel resting spine-up on a flat surface near a cell door, the cover facing down, the pages slightly splayed from use, flat institutional light from overhead.

scenes.narration: There is a moment, somewhere in the ninth month, that you will only recognize in retrospect — a Tuesday night count, the tier quiet, the key ring in your left hand, your pace exactly where it always is, and the thought arriving with no particular drama: you are good at this. Not proud of it. Not certain of what that goodness costs. Just the plain recognition that the job has become something you carry with competence, the way you carry the fourteen ounces of the key ring without noticing anymore. The manual is still in your locker. You have not opened it in sixty days.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell standing alone at the end of the tier, facing down the corridor, the key ring in his left hand at his side, his posture still and upright, the corridor receding into the dim distance behind him, the cell doors all closed.

scenes.narration: In the mornings, driving home as the sky goes pale, you catch yourself clocking the stoplights — the exact interval between yellow and red. You count the cars in the lot of the convenience store on Route 9. Four cars. Then a fifth pulling in. You do not realize you are counting. Your hands are on the wheel and the radio is on and you are counting. When you get home, Renata is already up, starting coffee, and she looks at you the way she sometimes looks at you now — taking a measurement she does not name — and you smile and tell her the drive was fine, and this is true, and only part of what is true.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CONTINUOUS] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of a commuter road scene at early dawn — a single car at a red light, the sky pale gray-pink above flat suburban rooflines, the driver's silhouette visible through the windshield.

scenes.narration: The rhythm is real. You do not choose it anymore — it moves through you the way a building's hum moves through the floor. Four a.m. count. Walk the tier. Log the check. Know the voices. Keep the three feet. Answer to Darnell when Curtis says it, because he says it the way someone says a name they mean. You are ten months in and the man you were in week one — the one who read the manual on his lunch break, who called the count in too loud, who checked the distance with his eyes — that man is not gone. He is just further back in the corridor now, behind you, somewhere past the flickering light above cell eleven.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of a long empty corridor receding into deep shadow behind the frame's near edge, a single fluorescent strip flickering above a cell door in the distance, the perspective drawn as if the viewer is moving away from that point — the light getting smaller, the shadow getting wider.

scenes.narration: Level three, the architecture.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of a man in civilian clothes sitting at a kitchen table at an odd hour, a mug of coffee in front of him, staring at nothing, the kitchen window showing deep night outside, a woman's hand resting on the table near his — not touching, almost.

scenes.narration: It is the middle of your second year, and you have stopped noticing the drive to work. Not the route — you can still tell someone every turn — but the act of it, the intention of it. Your hands find the wheel. The radio plays something you do not register. You arrive in the parking lot and you are already counting: eleven cars in your row, three empty spaces near the light post, the distance from your trunk to the facility entrance in footsteps you have measured before and will measure again without deciding to. The counting is not a habit you chose. It is what the job left behind in the part of your brain that used to rest.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of a correctional facility parking lot before dawn, rows of cars lit by flat overhead security lights, a single dark-olive-uniformed figure — Darnell — walking from his car toward the facility entrance, head slightly down, the building's pale institutional face ahead of him.

scenes.narration: Your days off have started to feel structurally wrong. Not unpleasant — just off-shaped, like a room where the ceiling is six inches too high and you can never explain why you are uneasy. On a Saturday in November you sit in the living room for two hours and do almost nothing, and Renata comes in and asks what you want for dinner and you say you don't mind, which is true, but what you do not say is that you keep glancing at the clock at intervals that make no sense outside the unit — roughly every thirty minutes, the length of a count. You are not counting your own house. You are just noticing that you could.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell in a civilian t-shirt and sweatpants sitting on a living room couch, leaning slightly forward with his elbows on his knees, staring at a clock on the wall, warm afternoon light filling the room — a comfortable domestic space that he nonetheless occupies like someone waiting for something to begin.

scenes.narration: The sleep inversion happened so gradually you cannot locate the moment it completed. You were always a night-shift worker — you knew that going in — but there is a difference between working nights and being nocturnal in your whole animal self. Now it is two in the afternoon on your day off and you wake up in a room full of ordinary daylight and it feels like being caught in someone else's house. The coffee maker goes on at three p.m. Renata stopped commenting on it in September. You are not sure if that means she has accepted it or simply decided to wait.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CONTINUOUS] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of a bedroom across the span of a single day: midday light, curtains drawn, a figure sleeping; then late afternoon, the curtains beginning to glow warmer; then early evening, the figure sitting on the edge of the bed with the lamp on, the window outside already dark.

scenes.narration: The counting is not only at home. You are in a grocery store in March — a Wednesday, mid-morning, the aisles nearly empty — and you are counting the ceiling tiles in the produce section. Not loudly, not consciously, just your eyes moving along the grid the way they move along the tier. Twelve across, nine deep. You know this without having decided to know it. You notice a flicker in the third fluorescent strip from the back wall and your body registers it the same way it registers the bad bulb in C-corridor — as a maintenance note, as something that belongs to someone to fix. You put oranges in your cart and keep moving, and it is only in the parking lot that you think: I just ran a count on a grocery store.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of a bright grocery store interior, wide aisles, fluorescent ceiling panels overhead in a visible grid, a lone figure — Darnell in civilian clothes, a shopping cart beside him — standing in the produce section with his eyes tilted slightly upward toward the ceiling, surrounded by ordinary shoppers in soft focus.

scenes.narration: There are other small migrations. You have started watching yellow traffic lights — not to decide whether to stop, but timing the interval between yellow and red the way you time the interval between a man's request and what he actually needs. Four seconds, five, sometimes three on the short ones. You sit at a red light on Route 9 and notice you are holding your breath in the exact measure you hold it during a welfare check — just enough suspension to listen for something on the other side. Renata is in the passenger seat. She asks if you are tired. You say you are fine. Both of those things are partially true.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon close-up of a car's dashboard and windshield at night, a traffic light glowing yellow in the upper center of the frame, Darnell's hands resting on the steering wheel in the foreground, his face barely visible in reflection on the glass — composed, distant, watching.

scenes.narration: Renata notices the three-foot thing before she has a name for it. She will tell you this later, much later, in a way that is not an accusation — just an observation she has been holding. She noticed it at a party in October, a neighbor's backyard, adults and kids and somebody's dog and music from a phone propped in a planter, and you stood at the perimeter of the yard all evening near the fence, watching the space. Not uncomfortably. Not visibly wrong. But always with three feet between you and anyone who approached, always with your back near something solid. She thought at first you were tired. Then she thought it was just how you stood now. By December she understood it was not a mood.

scenes.narration: On the unit, Curtis calls you by your first name the way he always has, and the familiarity still sits in you in the complicated way it always has — not warmth exactly, not resistance exactly, something that has no name in the manual. He asks once, in the flat tone of someone who asks because asking is one of the few things left to do, whether you sleep okay. You say you do. He nods once, slowly, like a man who knows what people say when they want to end a conversation, and returns to whatever he was reading. You walk the rest of the tier. You do not count the steps. You have already counted them.

Flat cartoon illustration of a death row corridor at night, Darnell walking the tier in his dark olive uniform, the long row of cell doors on either side under thin blue overhead light, one cell slightly more warmly lit than the others — a suggestion of a lamp or a reading light, a figure just visible at the bars.

scenes.narration: What the unit has given you is not paranoia and not fear and not even quite hypervigilance, though people will use that word later when they have a reason to name it. It is more like a new instrument of attention — a way of reading a room that starts at the perimeter, works inward, and does not settle until it has located every variable. Your home is not a threat. The grocery store is not a threat. You know this fully, in the part of yourself that reasons. But the instrument doesn't turn off. It runs in the background the way a building's ventilation runs — constant, structural, and only audible in the quiet. The quiet, these days, is most of what your days off are.

Flat cartoon illustration of a domestic living room at night, a single lamp casting a cone of light in the corner, Darnell sitting in an armchair with his hands loosely in his lap and his eyes open, the room around him rendered in soft dark geometry — furniture, doorways, windows — as if the space itself has been quietly measured and filed.

scenes.narration: It is a Sunday in late January, and Renata sits across from you at the kitchen table and says, quietly, not as a confrontation: you're not all the way here anymore. She doesn't mean it as a complaint — her voice is level, almost careful, the voice of a person who has chosen the right moment. You look at your coffee mug and then at her and you say: I know. It is the most accurate thing you have said in months. She reaches across the table — not quite to your hand, almost — and you think about the three feet. You think about the manual. You think about how neither of those things prepared you for a kitchen table in January, and how the geometry of the unit is inside you now and you are not sure yet what that means for the geometry of everything else.

scenes.narration: Level four, the date.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Flat 2D cartoon close-up of a single sheet of paper on an institutional desk, a hand resting beside it, the paper blank of any text but clearly official — crisp corners, a single checkmark shape, the hand neither picking it up nor pushing it away.

scenes.narration: It is a Tuesday in February, and you know before you are told. You know the way you know a count is off before you finish running it — something in the weight of the hallway, the particular way the shift supervisor does not look at you when you sign in. By the time the lieutenant calls you in and sets the date on the table between you, the date that is nine weeks from now, you have already done something quiet inside yourself. Something preparatory. You sit across from him and you nod at the right moments and you do not ask to be removed from the assignment, and you will spend a long time afterward deciding whether that is because you are a professional or because you cannot name what removing yourself would mean.

scenes.narration: The unit changes. It does not announce the change — it shifts the way a room shifts when someone has moved a piece of furniture three inches to the left, and you keep walking into the space where the furniture used to be. New protocols layer onto old ones. The schedule compresses. A vocabulary enters the shift briefings that you have heard before in training but that now arrives with weight: the movement, the team, the witness room. These are not new words. They are the same words the manual used. But in the manual they were hypothetical, and now they have a date attached to them, and the date is nine weeks away and then eight and then seven.

scenes.narration: Curtis knows. Of course Curtis knows — the men on the tier know the procedural vocabulary as well as you do, in some cases better. You have been doing the 4 a.m. count for two years now and Curtis has been on this tier for six, and he has watched officers cycle through the way you might watch weather come and go. The week after the date is set, you walk past his cell at the 4 a.m. count and he says, good morning, Darnell, the way he always has, with that same flat courtesy he extends to you and to almost no one else. You say, morning, Curtis. You keep walking. The key ring is in your left hand and it weighs exactly what it has always weighed.

scenes.narration: The weeks compress in a way that weeks on the tier do not usually compress. You have spent two years here learning that time on the row moves differently — slower inside, faster outside, a quality of suspension that the men live inside and that you enter and exit twice a day at the shift boundary. But now the suspension is gone. Every shift has a countdown in it whether you mark it or not. You run the count. You walk the tier. You attend the briefings about the movement and the team assignments and the order of the witness room, and you take notes on a small yellow legal pad and the notes are clean and professional and you fold the pad shut when the briefing is over and you carry it back to your locker and you do not think about it again until the next briefing.
scenes.visual_prompt: Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Darnell in a folding chair at a briefing table, small yellow legal pad open, pen in hand. Darnell at his locker, back to the camera, folding the legal pad shut. Darnell at the tier door, key in the lock.

scenes.narration: At home, Renata watches you the way she has been watching you for a year now — with a specific quality of patience that you recognize as patience wearing thin. It is a Thursday in late February and she is making coffee at the counter and she asks how it is going on the unit, using that phrasing, on the unit, the phrasing she adopted six months ago when the words death row started to sit wrong in her mouth. You say it is fine. You say it is procedural. You hear yourself using that word — procedural — and you know she hears it too, the way you reach for it when you do not want to reach for anything else. She does not push. She sets the mug in front of you and her hand passes close to yours on the table, not touching, almost.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell in civilian clothes — a plain dark sweatshirt, no uniform — sitting at a kitchen table in early morning dimness, a coffee mug in front of him, Renata's partial figure at the counter in the background, her face turned slightly away, the kitchen window showing deep blue pre-dawn outside.

scenes.narration: Three weeks out, you attend a walk-through of the witness room. It is a small room. Smaller than you expected, though you are not sure what you expected — the manual has dimensions, and you have read the dimensions, but standing in the room is different from reading its dimensions in the same way that knowing a man's file is different from knowing that he has been calling you by your first name for two years. There is a large observation window along one wall. On the other side of it is the room where the procedure will happen. Both rooms are pale green. Both rooms are very clean. You stand in the witness room for approximately four minutes while the lieutenant talks through the sequence, and you look at the observation window, and your reflection is faint in the glass, and you look like yourself.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. scenes.narration: The last week is the longest and the shortest. You run every count. You walk every tier check. On the Wednesday before, Curtis asks you if you have eaten, because you have been losing weight and he has noticed, the way the men on the tier notice things from their position of absolute stillness, cataloguing the small changes in the people who move through their fixed world. You tell him you are fine. He says, all right, Darnell. He says it the same way he says good morning — flat, courteous, without performance. You think about the manual, which has seventeen pages on professional distance. You think about how the manual did not prepare you for a man who asks if you have eaten.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon close-up of a cell door's barred observation slot, warm low light pressing through from inside the cell, Darnell's profile just visible at the edge of the frame — standing close but not touching the door, his expression still, his eyes level with the slot.

scenes.narration: The night before, you cannot sleep. This is not unusual — you have been sleeping poorly since February — but tonight the sleeplessness has a different texture to it, less like the usual restlessness and more like waiting. You lie in the dark next to Renata and you listen to the house and you count the seconds between the sounds: the refrigerator compressor, the furnace, a car on the street outside. You count them the same way you count the seconds of the count. At 3:17 a.m. you get up and go to the kitchen and sit at the table without turning on the light. The mug from last night is still in the dish rack. Outside the window it is fully dark, and the street is empty, and in six hours you will drive to the facility and put on your uniform and do your job.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. scenes.narration: Level five, the witness room.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Flat 2D cartoon illustration of an institutional observation window set into a pale green wall, the glass dark and reflective, the corridor on the near side lit by a single overhead fluorescent strip, nothing visible through the glass yet.

scenes.narration: It is a Wednesday in November, and the temperature has dropped enough that your breath shows in the parking lot when you arrive at eleven at night. You are not on a regular shift. The scheduling supervisor called you two weeks ago and used the words 'the team,' and you said yes before you fully understood what you were saying yes to. By the time you understood, the conversation was already over.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. scenes.narration: The briefing happens in a room you have never been in before, a room that is not on the tier, a room that smells faintly of carpet cleaner and old coffee. There are seven people in it. The supervisor speaks in a voice that is careful and entirely flat, the way a man's voice gets when he has said the same sentences many times and learned that the sentences go better without inflection. He uses the word 'procedure' eleven times. You count without meaning to.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell seated at a small conference table with several other uniformed figures, a supervisor standing at the head of the table, all faces turned toward him, Darnell's expression steady and inward, the fluorescent ceiling light harsh and even.

scenes.narration: Before the movement, you walk the tier one more time. Curtis is in his cell. He is sitting on the edge of his bunk with his hands on his knees, the same way he sits when he is thinking through something he does not want to think through. He has been calling you Darnell for almost three years. Tonight he does not call you anything. He looks at you, and the look is not accusing and it is not grateful and it is not asking for anything — it is simply the look of a man who has made his arrangements with the world and is waiting for the world to catch up. You nod. He nods. The tier is very quiet.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell standing in the corridor outside a barred cell door, the cell interior dimly lit, a figure seated on a bunk inside visible through the bars, both figures still, the overhead fluorescent buzzing its faint pale light across the pale green wall between them.

scenes.narration: The movement is exactly what the manual said it would be. You have read the protocol seventeen times since the call. You know where you stand, when you move, what you do not touch. Your body executes it cleanly. The training is a structure you can inhabit the way you inhabit the uniform, and for a while the structure holds you upright and keeps you somewhere slightly to the left of what is actually happening. This is, you will understand later, exactly what the structure was designed to do.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of a dark olive uniform hanging neatly on a hook against a plain institutional wall, pressed and complete, the hook casting a long thin shadow downward across the pale surface, no figure wearing it.

scenes.narration: The witness room is smaller than you expected. There is a viewing window and a row of chairs and a ceiling the same pale green as every other ceiling you have stood under in this building. You are standing, not sitting. The glass is thick — you know this from the manual, safety glass, rated — and the room on the other side is very bright and very still. The brightness is the thing you notice. The room on the other side is lit the way an operating theater is lit, the way nothing you have seen outside this building is ever lit: flat, complete, without shadow.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of the interior of the witness room, Darnell standing near the observation window, his back three-quarters to the viewer, the large glass panel ahead of him showing a brightly lit pale green room beyond, the stark contrast between the dim witness room and the over-lit chamber beyond, several empty chairs to his side.

scenes.narration: The procedure takes the time it takes. You will not remember the exact minutes afterward. What you remember is the sequence — the way one thing follows the next with a precision that felt, in the training, like order, and that feels now like something heavier than order, something that order was always a name for without naming. At a certain point the room on the other side of the glass becomes a room where something has happened. The overhead light does not change. The pale green walls do not change. But the room is different, and you are standing on the near side of the glass, and the glass is still there between you.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of the institutional chamber seen through the observation window glass, the room now empty of movement, a gurney under flat overhead light, the pale green walls perfectly still, the glass of the window faintly reflective — the ghost outline of Darnell visible as a reflection on the near surface of the glass, overlaid on the empty room beyond.

scenes.narration: The silence that follows is not an absence of sound. There are sounds — a chair scraping, a door, the ventilation system doing what it always does. The silence is a quality that sits inside the other sounds, the way cold sits inside a room even after you have turned on the heat. You have stood in quiet places before. The unit at four in the morning when the count is clean and every man on the tier is asleep. Your kitchen at home on Darnell's days off, before Renata is up. But this silence is a different register. You will spend the next several months trying to find a word for what it is, and you will not quite find it.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Flat cartoon illustration of an empty institutional corridor, no figures, all cell doors closed, the fluorescent overhead light humming its flat light across the pale green floor, a faint vibration line suggested in the ceiling fixture — the image of sound in a perfectly still space.

scenes.narration: You change out of the uniform in the locker room. Your regular clothes feel thin. You have worn them a thousand times — the dark gray henley, the worn-in jeans — and they have always felt like your clothes, the texture of your own life. Tonight they feel like a costume, like something a person wears to suggest that they live somewhere other than this building, and you are not sure the suggestion is convincing. You tie your shoes. You check the locker twice without knowing why.
scenes.visual_prompt: Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. [QUICK_CUTS] Flat cartoon close-up sequence: a locker door swinging open; a folded dark olive uniform set down on a bench; civilian clothes — gray henley, denim — being pulled on by Darnell's hands; a shoelace being tied, slowly; the locker door swinging closed.

scenes.narration: It is a little before five in the morning when you get to your car. The temperature has dropped further; the windshield is fogged from the inside before you have even started the engine. You drive. You are not driving home. You are not driving anywhere in particular, and then you are pulling into the parking lot of a gas station on Route 9 that is open and lit and completely empty. You pull into a space facing the glass front of the station. Inside you can see the rows of packaged food under their fluorescent light, the clerk at the counter reading something, a rotating rack of sunglasses nobody is looking at. You turn off the engine. You do not go in.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene.
