Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell's car parked facing a gas station storefront in the very early morning darkness, the station interior brightly lit through the large glass front windows, the shelves and counter faintly visible inside, Darnell a still silhouette in the driver's seat, the lot otherwise empty, no other vehicles.

scenes.narration: The manual prepared you for the procedure. Every checklist, every protocol, every measured sentence in the briefing was designed to carry you through the procedure intact, and it worked — you are intact. You said yes when you were supposed to, you stood where the manual said to stand, you kept the three feet. What the manual did not have a section for is this parking lot, this engine ticking as it cools, this specific quality of fluorescent light at five in the morning that looks almost exactly like the light in the room on the other side of the glass. You sit with that for a while. It is November. The windows are still fogging at the edges. You are thirty-one years old, and the silence inside this car is the same silence as the silence inside, and you are learning, slowly, that you will carry both of them now.

Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell in the driver's seat of his parked car, seen from the passenger side, hands folded in his lap, face turned slightly toward the gas station light, expression inward and very still, the fogged window edges framing him, the pre-dawn dark pressing against every window, the gas station glow casting a faint pale rectangle across his face.

scenes.narration: Level six, the afterward.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Flat cartoon illustration of a guard standing at the end of an empty corridor, all cell doors closed, early morning light pressing through a single high institutional window at the far end, the long corridor between the figure and the light filled with flat shadow.

scenes.narration: Three days after, you go back. You sign in at the same desk, hang your jacket on the same hook, and walk the same tier you have walked for two years. The count at four in the morning is still the count at four in the morning. You call each number and a voice answers, and you mark it, and you move on. The procedure does not change because you have changed. This is, you will come to understand, both the difficulty of the job and its mercy.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell, a Black man in a dark olive correctional officer uniform with a utility belt, walking a long corridor of closed cell doors under fluorescent light, a clipboard held at his side, his posture even and deliberate, the corridor receding behind him.

scenes.narration: There is a new man on the tier by February. His name is Jerome, and he does not speak for the first two weeks except to answer count. You have seen this before — not the specifics, but the shape of it, the way a man folds himself down to the minimum until he understands what the space will allow. You do not try to open him up. You run your count and you move on, and you let the silence between you be a thing he can trust.
scenes.visual_prompt: [CLOSE-UP] Flat cartoon close-up of a hand gripping a clipboard, a short list of marks visible on the sheet, the hand relaxed but deliberate, the edge of a cell door visible at the frame's left margin.

scenes.narration: Renata asks you on a Sunday in March, directly, the way she has been not asking for months. She sets down her coffee and she looks at you and she says: are you okay. Not as a formality. She means it as a question that expects a real answer, and she has been patient enough to wait until she thought you might be able to give one. You tell her something true — that you are sleeping better than you expected, that the job still makes sense to you, that you know how to do it. You tell her something incomplete. You do not tell her about the particular quality of the silence in the room that night, the way it had a texture, a weight, a temperature that the manual had no word for. You are not withholding this to protect her. You are withholding it because you do not yet have language that fits around it, and you have learned, in two years on this unit, that some things should not be spoken until the language is right.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell in civilian clothes sitting across a kitchen table from a woman, Renata, dark-haired, wearing a plain sweater, her coffee mug set aside, her eyes on his face — Darnell's expression steady, attentive, the slight pause of a man choosing his words with care, morning light coming through a window behind them.

scenes.narration: The months accumulate the way they always have on this unit — not by event but by repetition, by the small sediment of days that are mostly alike. You learn that Jerome takes his meals slowly and returns his tray without complaint. You learn that the man in the fourth cell has a sister who writes every week, and that he reads her letters standing up, his back to the door, which is his own business and you respect it. You are accumulating a particular kind of knowledge that has no transferable credential, no line on a resume. You know the difference between a man who is quiet because he is at peace and a man who is quiet because he has stopped expecting anything. You learned to make that distinction slowly, across two years, and now you make it in about thirty seconds.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Flat cartoon illustration of a long cell-lined corridor seen from mid-tier, Darnell's figure small and centered, multiple cell doors closed on both sides, the overhead light even and institutional, the space suggesting settled routine rather than tension.

scenes.narration: You notice, sometime in the spring of your third year on the unit, that you have stopped counting things outside. The parking spaces, the ceiling tiles, the seconds between yellow and red — those habits dissolved somewhere over the winter without you marking their departure. What replaced them is harder to name. Something more like attention. You find yourself watching people the way you watch the tier: not for danger, but for the thing just before the thing — the half-second of stillness that precedes a decision, the shift in a man's posture when something has changed inside him that he hasn't said aloud yet. Renata calls it unsettling and also says she trusts it. Those two things are both true, and you are at peace with them coexisting.
scenes.visual_prompt: [REACTION] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell in civilian clothes standing at a grocery store checkout line, other figures blurred and secondary behind him, Darnell's gaze calm and inward-facing, slightly elsewhere, a hand resting on the cart handle — a man whose attention has been trained to read rooms rather than stand in them.

scenes.narration: You are still good at the job. You run the count clean, you know the tier, you know which silences are neutral and which ones need checking. The newer officers ask you questions and you give them answers that are technically accurate and slightly insufficient, because the part of the answer that would actually help them cannot be transmitted in the break room. It has to be accumulated. It took you two years and one night in a witness room to learn what the manual was actually preparing you for, and you do not say this to them. You just tell them to keep their three feet, and to learn the voices before the faces, and to pay attention to the men who have stopped asking for things.
scenes.visual_prompt: [ESTABLISHING] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell standing in a small institutional break room, two younger officers seated at a table across from him, their posture attentive, Darnell's arms loosely crossed, his expression measured — a man sharing what he can and holding the rest.

scenes.narration: There are mornings — not every morning, but enough — when you pull into the facility parking lot and sit with the engine running a few seconds longer than you need to. Not because you don't want to go in. Because you have learned to mark the boundary. The outside silence and the inside silence are not the same silence, and the cost of treating them as equivalent is something you measured once and do not intend to measure again. You turn the engine off. You sit in the quiet. You are twenty-seven years old. You have been doing this for three years, and the man you were when you hung the uniform up for the first time is not quite the man who is going to take it off the hook this morning. You are not sure when the exchange happened. You are not sure it was a loss.
scenes.visual_prompt: [METAPHOR] Darnell is the main subject and protagonist in this scene. Depict Darnell as Guard On Death Row; any other people are secondary and visually distinct from Darnell. Flat cartoon illustration of Darnell seen from outside through a car windshield, sitting in the driver's seat in a facility parking lot, the engine off, the institutional building a flat pale shape behind him, early morning light gray and thin, his hands resting on the steering wheel, his eyes forward — a man in the space between two kinds of silence.

scripts.title: Your Life As A Guard On Death Row
scripts.topic_description: You arrive with a uniform and a manual, taught to measure distance between eyes and bars. Over time the rhythms of headcounts, last meals and visiting hours hollow into a quiet architecture of small mercies and tightened protocols, until the day you stand in the witness room and everything you were taught meets a human body. The ending is less a verdict than the slow rearrangement of how you listen to silence afterward.

scripts.title: Your Life As A Burger King Employee
scripts.topic_description: You take the job at sixteen for summer money and freedom—part-time crew, bringing home about $10k–$14k a year, thinking it's temporary. Years thicken: you slide into full-time shifts ($22k–$27k), become a shift lead ($28k–$34k), then an assistant manager ($34k–$40k), and finally the manager on the night roster ($38k–$48k), every promotion a softer lock. The comedy of burned fries and radio jingles gives way to the shabby peace of inertia: you told yourself 'one more year' so many times you forgot to leave.
